strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful idea: amortize virtual screening over combinatorial synthesis library structure by factorizing a learned molecular surrogate into reaction/R-group/synthon contributions, enabling exhaustive approximate top-k retrieval under constraints.

The method is technically coherent and well motivated for CSLs. The decomposition from surrogate embeddings to additive synthon associative contributions is clean, and the custom GPU top-k implementation addresses a real systems bottleneck rather than only proposing a model.

The authors provide a valuable benchmark-style dataset: a fully enumerated 12M-compound CSL with docking scores for five targets and physicochemical properties, allowing actual top-k recall evaluation rather than only qualitative enrichment.

Runtime results are compelling: the reported end-to-end GPU search times on a 10B-compound library, including constrained retrieval, demonstrate strong practical scalability for the approximate objective.

Presentation is generally clear, with helpful formalization of the retrieval problem, model factorization, and GPU search procedure. The paper is easy to follow despite combining cheminformatics, surrogate modeling, and systems implementation.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence is not yet strong enough for acceptance. On the fully labeled 12M library, true top-j recall is mixed rather than uniformly strong: recall drops substantially for stricter constraints and for some targets, and the factorized surrogate has only moderate docking-score R-squared, especially for ESR1/F10/MET. This weakens claims about reliably recovering the true best compounds.

The 10B-scale results mostly validate speed and predicted-score enrichment, not true retrieval quality. Because the 10B library is not exhaustively docked and the top retrieved compounds do not appear to be redocked or otherwise validated, the paper cannot show that the ultra-large search actually finds better true-scoring compounds rather than surrogate artifacts.

The comparison to prior screening algorithms is too limited. Thompson sampling is evaluated only on five reactions and only in the unconstrained setting, while other relevant methods mentioned in the introduction, such as V-SYNTHES and NGT-style approaches, are not empirically compared. This makes the significance relative to existing virtual screening workflows hard to judge.

The computational budget comparison is potentially unfair or at least under-explained. APEX requires a large labeled training set and surrogate/factorizer training before the fast search phase, but the main comparisons emphasize query-time top-k retrieval and do not fully account for offline docking, training cost, amortization break-even points, or the cost of adapting to new targets/objectives.

The benchmark library is explicitly not guaranteed to be synthetically feasible, despite the paper’s framing around make-on-demand CSLs. This is acceptable as a benchmark design choice, but it materially limits claims about immediate applicability to real purchasable/synthesizable libraries.

Generalization and leakage concerns remain. Training on a 1M downsampled CSL and evaluating on larger libraries generated from the same BRICS-derived reactions/fragments may test interpolation over shared chemistry more than robust extrapolation to new reactions, scaffolds, or vendor libraries.

Several methodological claims need more support, including the assertion that embedding noise addresses errors-in-variables issues. There are few ablations isolating the impact of noise, factorization quality, embedding dimension, training-set size, or factorizer architecture on downstream recall.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The manuscript says code and data links are provided, but the visible footnote is incomplete in the anonymized PDF, and important details such as training schedules, model architectures, dataset construction scripts, and exact split definitions are not sufficiently specified in the main text.

strengths: The paper has a clear and potentially useful idea: exploit the combinatorial structure of synthesis libraries to factor a multitask neural surrogate into synthon-level contributions, enabling very fast exhaustive top-k retrieval over predicted objectives and constraints.

The runtime engineering appears practically relevant. Reported end-to-end GPU runtimes on a T4, such as roughly 11-24 seconds for 10B compounds depending on k and constraints, suggest that the factorized top-k implementation could be useful if the surrogate predictions are trustworthy.

The authors attempt to improve reproducibility by constructing an open CSL benchmark and exhaustively annotating the 12M-compound version with docking scores and RDKit properties. The paper also evaluates multiple targets and several medicinal-chemistry constraint sets.
weaknesses: The central scientific claim is not adequately supported because the method optimizes approximate surrogate scores, while the evidence that these scores identify truly good compounds is weak. Figure 7 shows only moderate or poor R-squared for several docking endpoints, especially after factorization, with targets such as MET, ESR1, and F10 appearing around or below the 0.4-0.5 range. This directly undermines the use of APEX for docking-driven virtual screening.

The 10B-compound results are largely self-referential: Figure 4 demonstrates enrichment according to APEX-predicted docking scores, not ground-truth docking scores. Since the paper cannot validate the 10B top hits with docking, it does not establish that the impressive runtime translates into useful scientific retrieval at the claimed scale.

Top-k recall on the fully annotated 12M library is mixed rather than consistently strong. In Figure 3, recall@100k falls substantially for stricter constraints and larger j, and some target/constraint combinations retrieve only a small fraction of the true top set. The conclusion overstates these results as high recall and effective constraint satisfaction.

The comparison to Thompson sampling is too limited to support broad claims. It is only unconstrained, only covers the five largest reactions, omits several relevant baselines discussed in the introduction, and does not clearly establish a fair accounting of training labels, surrogate pretraining cost, and expensive oracle evaluations.

The benchmark CSL is not guaranteed synthetically feasible, despite the motivation being make-on-demand combinatorial synthesis libraries. This weakens the connection between the experimental setting and the drug-discovery use case the paper emphasizes.

Methodological details needed for reproducibility are incomplete. The code footnote appears to have a missing URL, hyperparameters and training details are sparse, the docking protocol is not described in enough detail to reproduce the labels, and it is unclear whether the very large datasets and model weights are actually accessible.

The treatment of limitations and ethics is inadequate. The paper does not seriously discuss risks from optimizing noisy docking surrogates, false-positive enrichment, synthetic infeasibility, applicability limits across library designs, or the costs and biases introduced by the training labels. The LLM-use statement is present but minimal.

strengths: The paper makes a clear and practically meaningful contribution: APEX turns top-k search over combinatorial synthesis libraries into a fast approximate exhaustive search by factorizing surrogate embeddings over reaction/R-group/synthon structure. The formulation is well motivated and the computational advantage is substantial.

The evaluation includes a useful open benchmark CSL with exhaustive docking/property annotations for the 12M-compound setting, enabling direct recall-at-k comparisons against true top-j sets under multiple targets and drug-likeness constraints.

Runtime evidence is compelling: the reported end-to-end GPU search over a 10B-compound library in roughly 11-24 seconds on a Tesla T4, depending on k and constraints, supports the scalability claim for the factorized search stage.

The method is compared against random search and Thompson sampling with matched evaluation budgets; APEX generally matches or outperforms TS, especially at lower budgets, while also naturally supporting property constraints.
The paper is mostly well written, with a clean mathematical presentation, clear figures, implementation details for the GPU top-k operator, and a reasonable LLM-use disclosure.
weaknesses: The strongest empirical validation of retrieval accuracy is limited to the 12M fully scored benchmark. For the 10B library, the paper shows enrichment according to predicted/surrogate scores, but does not verify retrieved compounds with ground-truth docking, so the central ultra-large-library claim is less fully validated than the runtime claim.

Surrogate quality is uneven: Figure 7 shows relatively modest R-squared values for several docking targets, and the factorized surrogate is sometimes worse than the original surrogate. Since APEX depends directly on these approximations, the paper would benefit from a more explicit analysis of approximation error, false negatives, and when retrieval may fail.

The benchmark CSL is constructed with BRICS recombination and explicitly does not ensure synthetic feasibility, which limits conclusions about direct applicability to real make-on-demand libraries despite the relevance of the CSL abstraction.

Baselines are somewhat narrow. The TS comparison is restricted to the top five reactions and to unconstrained objectives because the implementation lacks constraint support, while other relevant large-library screening approaches discussed in the introduction are not empirically compared.

The limitations and ethics discussion is thin. The paper notes lack of synthetic-feasibility guarantees in the benchmark, but does not deeply discuss downstream medicinal-chemistry validity, docking-score limitations, possible misuse, or biases introduced by the constructed library and surrogate training data.

Reproducibility is promising but not fully assessable from the manuscript text: it states that code and dataset/model links are provided, but the visible footnote appears incomplete/anonymized, and important training details such as architectures, optimization settings, and hardware/precomputation costs are only lightly specified.

strengths: The core idea is clear and useful: factorizing a learned molecular surrogate into cached per-synthon contributions exploits CSL structure and turns approximate top-k retrieval into a fast exhaustive pass over the combinatorial library.

The paper provides a reasonably sound methodological formulation, including the surrogate/factorizer decomposition, constraint handling through lexicographic ranking of violation and objective, and implementation details for scalable GPU top-k retrieval.

The empirical results support the main computational efficiency claim: reported end-to-end GPU search over 10B compounds takes tens of seconds, and scaling to a 70B Enamine REAL library is demonstrated.

The benchmark construction is valuable for the community: a fully enumerated and docked 12M-compound CSL with multiple docking targets and physicochemical endpoints enables ground-truth top-k recall evaluation.
Presentation is generally strong. The motivation, algorithmic pipeline, mathematical notation, runtime table, and appendices with model/training details are easy to follow.

Originality is good: the paper adapts factorization-style ideas to combinatorial synthesis library screening in a way that appears practically distinct from standard active learning, generative, and synthon-based search methods.
weaknesses: The evaluation is narrower than the paper's broad claims. The only rigorous top-k recall evaluation is on the authors' constructed BRICS-derived library, which explicitly does not ensure synthetic feasibility, while the real Enamine experiment only shows enrichment against random/background samples rather than ground-truth recall or stronger validation.

Baselines are limited. The main comparison is Thompson sampling on only the five largest reactions and in the unconstrained setting; there is no substantive comparison to active-learning virtual screening methods such as Deep Docking/MolPal-style approaches, hierarchical synthon screening, or standard surrogate scoring with approximate pruning under matched compute.

The central retrieval quality is constrained by surrogate accuracy, and the paper does not fully quantify when the approximation fails. Some docking endpoints and zero-shot Enamine results show degraded predictive performance, but the implications for false positives, false negatives, and downstream oracle cost are not deeply analyzed.

The claims around arbitrary objectives/constraints are somewhat stronger than demonstrated: APEX can recombine already-trained endpoints declaratively, but new expensive objectives still require labeled data and surrogate training, and constraint satisfaction is based on predicted rather than true constraints.

Reproducibility is promising but incomplete from the manuscript alone. It states that code, data, and weights are available, and gives architecture/training details, but the exact repository link is not visible in the manuscript text, and large-scale reproduction depends on substantial datasets, docking artifacts, and custom CUDA code.

The limitations and ethics discussion is thin. The manuscript acknowledges lack of synthetic feasibility for the constructed benchmark, but does not include a dedicated limitations section discussing docking-score reliability, applicability domain, chemical validity/synthesizability on real campaigns, compute/data requirements, or dual-use risks in molecular discovery.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical bottleneck: repeated top-k search over very large combinatorial synthesis libraries under changing objectives and constraints. The proposed factorized surrogate is a natural and potentially useful way to exploit CSL structure and amortize inference over synthons rather than enumerated products.

The method is clearly described mathematically, including the surrogate, factorizer, additive synthon contributions, constraint handling, and GPU top-k implementation. The runtime measurements are concrete and impressive, e.g. sub-30 second top-1M retrieval on a 10B library on a T4 GPU.

The authors attempt to improve reproducibility by constructing an open BRICS-derived benchmark with exhaustive labels for the 1M and 12M libraries, and they evaluate multiple protein targets and several property-constraint sets rather than only a single toy objective.
The appendix gives useful architectural and training details, endpoint definitions, constraint definitions, and additional analyses such as regression performance and error decomposition.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence is not strong enough for the scale of the claims. Ground-truth top-k recall is only evaluated on the 12M synthetic BRICS library, while the headline 10B and 70B results mainly show enrichment or predicted retrieval speed, not verified recovery of true top compounds. This leaves the ultra-large-library effectiveness claim only partially supported.

The benchmark library is explicitly not checked for synthetic feasibility, despite the paper being framed around make-on-demand CSLs. This is a serious mismatch with the motivating application, since the method's value depends on structured, synthesizable combinatorial spaces.

Surrogate accuracy for docking is modest, especially after factorization and in the zero-shot Enamine setting. Figure 6 shows substantial drops for several targets, and Figure 2 recall is often far from high for stringent constraints or larger top-j sets. Since APEX can only retrieve what the surrogate ranks well, these errors materially weaken the screening claims.

The baselines are insufficient. The main retrieval plots emphasize comparison to random selection, which is too weak. The Thompson sampling comparison is restricted to only the five largest reactions, unconstrained settings, and selected budgets, while stronger active-learning, pruning, or dense-retrieval baselines discussed in related work are not empirically compared.

The Enamine REAL experiment is especially under-evidenced: the model is applied zero-shot to a proprietary 70B library with only a 100k random background distribution and no oracle top-k reference, no calibrated uncertainty, and no clear analysis of domain shift beyond regression plots. Claims of generality therefore feel premature.

The treatment of constraints is not fully convincing. Constraint satisfaction is reported for APEX-predicted retrievals, but the paper does not sufficiently analyze false positives/false negatives under true constraints, feasibility of post-filtering, or how errors in multiple constraints compound in realistic screening workflows.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as provided. The code link appears placeholder-like, and the availability of the generated libraries, docking labels, trained weights, exact splits, and CUDA implementation is asserted only vaguely. Without these artifacts, the main benchmark and speed claims would be difficult to independently verify.

The paper has almost no limitations discussion. It does not adequately acknowledge dependence on surrogate quality, lack of experimental validation, limitations of docking scores as labels, possible chemical invalidity or poor synthesizability of the BRICS library, and the cost of generating labeled training data.

The impact/ethics discussion is perfunctory. For a drug-discovery paper, it should at least discuss risks from unreliable docking surrogates, potential misuse or overinterpretation of virtual hits, and the difference between computational enrichment and experimentally validated therapeutic utility.

strengths: Significant and timely contribution: APEX addresses a real bottleneck in ultra-large combinatorial synthesis library screening by exploiting CSL structure to make exhaustive surrogate scoring and top-k retrieval practical at 10B-70B scale.

Technically sound core idea: the additive factorization of surrogate embeddings into cached synthon/R-group/reaction contributions is well motivated, leads to clear computational savings, and is paired with an efficient GPU top-k implementation.

Strong empirical case for the intended computational task: the paper evaluates retrieval on a fully enumerated 12M-compound benchmark with ground-truth docking/property labels, reports recall under multiple objectives and drug-likeness constraints, compares against Thompson sampling, and provides convincing runtime measurements on 10B and 70B libraries.

Useful benchmark/data contribution: the fully enumerated BRICS-derived CSL with docking scores across five targets and many physicochemical properties is valuable for evaluating virtual screening methods with known top-k sets.
Presentation is generally clear, with a coherent problem formulation, readable derivations, helpful figures, and sufficient architectural/training detail in the appendix to understand the method.
weaknesses: The strongest retrieval accuracy claims are validated only on the constructed 12M BRICS benchmark; the 10B and Enamine 70B experiments mainly show enrichment rather than recall against true top compounds, so the evidence for real ultra-large-library top-k accuracy is indirect.

The benchmark CSL is explicitly not guaranteed to be synthetically feasible, which weakens the connection between the main fully supervised evaluation and make-on-demand chemical libraries, even though the Enamine experiment partially mitigates this.

Baselines are limited: Thompson sampling is evaluated only on the top five reactions and without constraints, while comparisons to active-learning/deep-docking style methods or dense-retrieval methods are mostly qualitative.

The method inherits errors from both the docking oracle and learned surrogate; top-k recall can remain modest for the most selective settings, and there is no experimental or prospective validation that retrieved molecules are biologically meaningful hits.

Reproducibility is promising but incomplete in the manuscript: code/data/model weights are said to be available via a repository/README, but the manuscript does not provide enough concrete access details, and the proprietary Enamine 70B experiment may not be fully reproducible for all readers.

Limitations and broader impacts are underdeveloped. Important caveats around docking-score reliability, synthetic feasibility, dependence on CSL structure, applicability to new objectives requiring labels, and possible misuse/dual-use in chemical design should be discussed more explicitly.
